topics.title: Chapter 27 — Memory Hierarchy
topics.summary: A computer does not store every useful byte in one uniformly fast place. It uses a hierarchy of storage technologies and structures with different capacities, access costs, and management rules. Programs perform well when frequently needed information remains in the levels that can serve it efficiently. This chapter uses qualitative relationships rather than a table of supposedly universal nanosecond values. Actual latency and bandwidth depend on the processor, memory configuration, access pattern, contention, power state, and measurement method. Treat hardware specifications and local measurements as evidence for a particular machine, not as constants of the language. [ R3 , R30 ]

topics.title: 27.1 Registers
topics.summary: Registers hold operands and execution state directly used by instructions. The compiler allocates many frequently used values to registers, subject to instruction constraints and calling conventions. Values that cannot remain in registers may be spilled to memory. A source-level local variable is not automatically a stack slot. It can live in a register, be folded into another expression, or disappear when it has no observable effect. Looking at generated assembly is the appropriate way to investigate a particular compiled implementation.

topics.title: 27.2 L1 cache
topics.summary: An L1 cache is a small, fast cache close to an execution core. Processors commonly distinguish instruction and data L1 caches, although exact organizations vary. Its limited capacity favors compact working sets and repeated access to nearby data. The cost of an L1 hit is not simply the cost of a complete source statement. Dependencies, execution ports, translation, and instruction scheduling also affect progress. A chain of dependent loads behaves differently from many independent loads that hardware can overlap.

topics.title: 27.3 L2 cache
topics.summary: L2 provides additional capacity beyond L1 at a different access cost. It can satisfy requests for lines absent from L1 without requiring a trip to main memory. Whether an L2 is private to a core or shared is a hardware design choice. A working set too large for L1 can still perform well when it fits in L2 and has predictable access. Performance often changes gradually or in steps as working-set size crosses hierarchy boundaries, rather than following a single universal “memory access” time.

topics.title: 27.4 L3 cache
topics.summary: An L3 or last-level cache often provides larger shared capacity, but names and sharing arrangements are not universal. Shared caches allow data to serve multiple cores while also creating competition for capacity and bandwidth. Cache inclusion policies vary. Do not assume that every line in a private cache must also exist in the last-level cache, or that evicting a line has identical consequences on all processors. For application design, focus first on working-set size, sharing patterns, and measured behavior.

topics.title: 27.5 DRAM
topics.summary: DRAM supplies main-memory capacity beyond the processor caches. Access cost depends on more than a single chip latency: memory controllers, channels, banks, row state, access concurrency, and NUMA placement can all matter. Bandwidth and latency limits are distinct. A workload with many independent sequential accesses may approach a bandwidth limit, while a dependent pointer-chasing workload may be limited by the latency of each next address. The same number of bytes can therefore take different times under different dependency patterns.

topics.title: 27.8 Latency

For example, following linked-list pointers often prevents the next address from being known in advance. Report the operation being measured. Cache-hit load latency, end-to-end request latency, and storage-read latency describe different boundaries. A number without its start event, end event, and conditions is difficult to interpret.

topics.title: 27.9 Throughput
topics.summary: Throughput is completed work per unit time. A system can have high throughput while individual requests experience substantial latency, especially when many operations overlap. Conversely, a fast isolated operation can yield poor aggregate throughput when shared resources serialize it. Useful units include bytes per second, records per second, and requests per second. Choose a unit tied to completed useful work, not merely to internal activity. Counting retries or duplicated work as successful throughput can conceal a broken design.

topics.title: 27.10 Capacity
topics.summary: Capacity is the amount of information a level can hold. Larger capacity can reduce misses, but only for data that remains useful before eviction. A cache filled with streaming data that will never be reused may displace a smaller, more valuable working set. Working-set analysis asks how much data is actively needed over a relevant interval. Total dataset size alone does not answer that question. A terabyte dataset processed in small independent tiles can have a modest active working set.

topics.title: 27.11 Cost
topics.summary: Cost includes hardware expense, energy, area, management overhead, and opportunity cost. Faster storage structures are constrained by more than purchase price. A design that used the fastest possible storage for every byte would face physical and economic limitations. The hierarchy is therefore a resource-allocation strategy. Software participates by making reuse visible, avoiding unnecessary movement, and organizing work so that scarce fast capacity holds valuable information. Optimization is often about moving fewer bytes rather than executing a cleverer arithmetic instruction.

LECTURE NARRATION
A computer does not store every useful byte in one uniformly fast place. It uses a hierarchy of storage technologies and structures with different capacities, access costs, and management rules. Programs perform well when frequently needed information remains in the levels that can serve it efficiently. This chapter uses qualitative relationships rather than a table of supposedly universal nanosecond values. Actual latency and bandwidth depend on the processor, memory configuration, access pattern, contention, power state, and measurement method. Treat hardware specifications and local measurements as evidence for a particular machine, not as constants of the language. [ R3 , R30 ]

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.
